questions.stem: The Cramér-Rao lower bound says that for an unbiased estimator $\hat{\theta}$ of $\theta$ based on $n$ i.i.d. observations:

options.text: $\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) \ge 1/(n\,I(\theta))$, where $I(\theta)$ is the Fisher information of one observation.
options.explanation: The Cramér-Rao bound: no unbiased estimator can have variance smaller than $1/(nI(\theta))$. An estimator achieving this bound is efficient.
This is the reciprocal of the correct bound. More information (larger $I(\theta)$) means a smaller achievable variance, not a larger one.
Zero variance would mean the estimator equals $\theta$ exactly regardless of the data — impossible when $\theta$ is unknown.
The Cramér-Rao bound is about variance, not bias. An unbiased estimator has $E[\hat{\theta}] = \theta$ by assumption.

questions.stem: The Neyman-Pearson lemma says the most powerful test at level $\alpha$ of $H_0: \theta = \theta_0$ vs $H_1: \theta = \theta_1$ is based on:

options.text: The likelihood ratio $\Lambda = L(\theta_1)/L(\theta_0)$, rejecting $H_0$ when $\Lambda > c_\alpha$.
options.explanation: This is the Neyman-Pearson lemma. No other test at the same significance level has higher power. Many standard tests (t-test, z-test) are special cases.

options.text: The sample mean $\bar{X}$, rejecting when $\bar{X}$ is too large.
options.explanation: For testing a Normal mean, this IS the likelihood ratio test — but the Neyman-Pearson lemma covers any simple vs simple hypothesis pair, not just Normal means.

options.text: Minimising the Type II error probability, ignoring Type I error.
options.explanation: The Neyman-Pearson framework controls Type I error at level $\alpha$ first, then maximises power (minimises Type II error) subject to that constraint.

options.text: The maximum likelihood estimator: reject $H_0$ when $\hat{\theta}_{MLE}$ is far from $\theta_0$.
options.explanation: While related, this is not the Neyman-Pearson lemma. The lemma specifies the likelihood ratio test, not a test based on the MLE.

questions.stem: A Markov chain has transition matrix $P = \begin{pmatrix} 0.7 & 0.3 \\ 0.4 & 0.6 \end{pmatrix}$. Which vector $\pi$ is a stationary distribution?

options.explanation: The first row of $P$, not the stationary distribution. Check: $(0.7)(0.7) + (0.3)(0.4) = 0.49 + 0.12 = 0.61 \ne 0.7$.
Check: $(0.5)(0.7) + (0.5)(0.4) = 0.55 \ne 0.5$. Equal distribution is only stationary if the chain is doubly stochastic (all column sums = 1), which it is not here.
Starting entirely in state 1, after one step you have $(0.7, 0.3) \ne (1,0)$.
